column3: The Hebrew leaves David unnamed in the opening clause and says Jonathan’s soul was bound to David’s soul. BSB supplies David and makes the two souls a combined subject; it renders the final “his soul” as “himself.”
The Hebrew leaves David unnamed and says Saul took him “on that day”; BSB supplies David and says “from that day.”
The Hebrew says Jonathan and David “cut a covenant”; BSB says Jonathan “made a covenant with David.” The final love expression literally refers to “his soul.”
The Hebrew has plural “his garments”; BSB uses singular “his tunic.”
The Hebrew twice uses “in the eyes” for the people and Saul’s servants; BSB combines both under one “in the sight.” It renders the servants as “officers.”
The Hebrew leaves the arriving group unnamed; BSB supplies “the troops” and “home.” The Hebrew names joy, where BSB makes this “joyful songs.”
The Hebrew says the women answered and said; BSB combines these into “sang out.”
The Hebrew says this “word” was evil in Saul’s eyes; BSB specifies “this song” and renders the eyes image as resentment.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew calls it an “evil spirit of God”; BSB has “a spirit of distress sent from God.” It names David’s playing hand without naming the instrument, where BSB supplies the harp.
The Hebrew explicitly says Saul hurled “the spear” and introduces his words with “said”; BSB uses “he hurled it” and “thinking.” It repeats David as the one evading him.
The Hebrew says the LORD was “with him”; BSB supplies David’s name.
The Hebrew says he “went out and came in before the people”; BSB expands this to leading troops out to battle and back.
The Hebrew names David and joins his success and the LORD’s presence with “and”; BSB uses “he” and makes the LORD’s presence an explicit “because” clause.
The Hebrew says Saul saw that “he” was successful; BSB supplies David.
The Hebrew says David was “going out and coming in before them”; BSB expands this to leading them out to battle and back.
The Hebrew introduces Saul’s private words with “said” and says his hand should not be against David; BSB has “was thinking” and adds the action of raising the hand.
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew actively says unnamed people told Saul, and that the matter was right in his eyes. BSB uses passive “was reported” and renders the eyes image as “it pleased him.”
The Hebrew says “I will give her to him”; BSB supplies David. It introduces the statement with “said,” rendered “thought” in BSB.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says Saul’s servants spoke “in David’s ears”; BSB simply says they relayed the words to him.
The Hebrew explicitly calls them “Saul’s servants” and quotes their report. BSB leaves the possessive implicit and makes the report indirect.
The Hebrew says Saul planned to cause David to “fall into the hand of the Philistines”; BSB makes the death explicit and uses plural “hands.”
The Hebrew says “the days were not full”; BSB specifies “Before the wedding day arrived.” It also renders the matter being right in David’s eyes as his being pleased.
The Hebrew repeats David’s name for bringing the foreskins; BSB uses “He.” In the final giving of Michal, the Hebrew uses “him,” where BSB supplies David.
The Hebrew separately says Saul saw and knew; BSB combines these as “realized.” It calls Michal “Saul’s daughter” and refers to the one loved as “him”; BSB has “his daughter” and names David.
The Hebrew names Saul at the start of his increasing fear; BSB uses “he.”
The Hebrew first says the commanders went out, then speaks of each time they went out; BSB combines these into one time clause and supplies “for battle.”
